issues.legal_issue: An earlier declaration of a monument as protected remains effective when a later notification purporting to supersede it was not published as required.
material_facts: A notification declared the monument a protected monument under the earlier preservation law.
A later notification purported to supersede the earlier one but was not published in the Official Gazette.
The later notification therefore did not satisfy the statutory publication requirement.
issues.conclusion: The later notification was ineffective, while the earlier notification remained effective and was saved by the repeal-and-saving provision of the later preservation law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 required the relevant notification to be published in the Official Gazette. Because the later notification was not so published, it did not supersede the earlier notification; the earlier declaration continued under Section 39(2) of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_against_injunction: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an injunction against construction near a protected monument.
predicates.earlier_protection_declaration: The government had earlier declared the monument protected under the applicable preservation law.
predicates.later_superseding_notice_unpublished: The government later issued a notice purporting to replace the earlier declaration but did not publish it as required.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerning construction near a protected monument involves an earlier protection declaration and an unpublished later notice purporting to replace it, the earlier declaration remains effective.

issues.legal_issue: A prohibition on construction near a protected monument is measured from the outer limit of the protected area, and a separate urban-planning law does not displace that prohibition.
material_facts: The monument's protection declaration identified a protected area, including its boundaries.
The construction plot was within 100 metres of the outer boundary of that protected area.
A municipal authority had sanctioned a building plan under urban-planning controls.
The restriction arose under legislation and rules directed to the preservation of protected monuments.
issues.conclusion: The 100-metre distance was to be measured from the outer boundary of the protected area, so construction on the plot was prohibited; the urban-planning law did not override that restriction.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 19 and 38 of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, and Rules 31 and 32 of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Rules, 1959, provide for restrictions on construction near protected monuments. The court held that the preservation law and the urban-planning law operated in different fields and that the preservation restriction governed; even if there were a conflict, the law specifically directed to protecting ancient monuments would prevail. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: appeal_against_construction_injunction and protected_area_has_outer_limit and plot_within_restricted_distance_of_outer_limit and urban_plan_approval

predicates.appeal_against_construction_injunction: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an injunction against construction near a protected monument.
predicates.protected_area_has_outer_limit: The monument's protection declaration identifies an area with an outer boundary.
predicates.plot_within_restricted_distance_of_outer: The proposed construction site lies within the distance restricted from the outer boundary of the protected area.
predicates.urban_plan_approval: An urban-planning authority sanctioned the proposed construction under its planning controls.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns construction within the restricted distance of a protected area's outer boundary, planning approval does not displace the monument-construction restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot direct the government to review a monument-protection notification merely to accommodate development where the notification implements the policy of preserving protected monuments.
material_facts: A court directed the government to review a notification restricting construction near protected monuments.
The notification had been issued to implement the policy of preserving monuments and archaeological sites.
The proposed review was connected to accommodating development and multistorey construction.
issues.conclusion: The direction to review the notification was unjustified and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Article 49 of the Constitution and the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 embody the policy of preserving protected monuments. Sections 19 and 38 of that Act and Rules 31 and 32 of the Rules support restrictions on construction near monuments. A court could not mandate review of such a restriction in the name of development. The court also noted that the later insertion of Sections 20A and 20B made the direction infructuous. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_against_mandamus_to_review_protec: The proceeding is an appeal from a court order directing the government to review a monument-protection notice.
predicates.notice_implements_monument_preservation: The government issued the notice to protect monuments or archaeological sites from construction-related harm.
predicates.review_sought_to_accommodate_development: The review was sought to allow or accommodate development despite the protective restriction.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a direction to review a notice issued to preserve monuments in order to accommodate development, the direction to review is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: Permission for construction in a prohibited area cannot be granted for a private project lacking larger public interest or for work that substantially harms the monument or its immediate surroundings.
material_facts: The proposed work was construction of a private multistorey building in an area subject to a construction prohibition.
The project was not shown to be a public work or a project essential to the public, or otherwise to serve a larger public interest.

The court interpreted the statutory exception as requiring that permitted work not substantially adversely affect preservation, safety, security, access, or the immediate surroundings of the monument.
issues.conclusion: The statutory exception cannot be used to permit private construction de hors public interest; public interest is central, and construction must not be permitted if it adversely affects the monument or its immediate surroundings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20A(3) of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 permits construction in a prohibited area only in exceptional cases, having regard to public interest, and subject to the statutory conditions, including the absence of substantial adverse impact. Read in light of Article 49 of the Constitution and the preservation purpose of the 1958 Act, the reference to other work or projects does not authorize construction for private interest alone. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: proceeding_interprets_exception_for_prohibited_area_construction and prohibited_area_construction and (not larger_public_interest or substantial_adverse_impact)

predicates.proceeding_interprets_exception_for_proh: The proceeding concerns the scope of an exception allowing work in an area where construction is generally prohibited.
predicates.prohibited_area_construction: A person proposes construction in an area where construction is generally barred to protect a monument.
predicates.larger_public_interest: The proposed work serves a public interest beyond the private interest of its owner or developer.
predicates.substantial_adverse_impact: The proposed work would substantially harm the monument's preservation, safety, security, access, or immediate surroundings.

issues.definition: When construction is proposed in a prohibited area, permission is not authorized if the project lacks larger public interest or would substantially harm the monument or its immediate surroundings.

issues.legal_issue: Repair or renovation of an existing building in a prohibited area does not include demolishing it and constructing a new building.
material_facts: The existing structure on the plot was demolished and foundation work began for a new building.
The statutory provision addressed repair or renovation of specified existing buildings in prohibited areas.
The court interpreted renovation in the context of the provision's reference to repair.
issues.conclusion: Renovation means work akin to repair and does not permit demolition of the existing structure and construction of a new one.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20C of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 permits an eligible owner to apply for repair or renovation of a qualifying existing building or structure in a prohibited area. The term renovation takes its colour from repair; it cannot be used to authorize demolition and reconstruction. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.proceeding_interprets_existing_building_: The proceeding concerns an exception allowing repair or renovation of an existing building in a prohibited area.
predicates.existing_building_in_prohibited_area: An existing building or structure is located in an area where construction is generally prohibited.
predicates.demolition_to_construct_new_building: The owner demolishes the existing building or structure in order to construct a new one.

issues.definition: When an existing building in a prohibited area is demolished to construct a new one, that work is not repair or renovation.
